title: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again)
note: The OS analogy (LLM = kernel, context window = RAM, tools = syscalls) and why your value is the app layer on top, not the model.

title: Taste & Craft: Tuomas Artman (CTO Linear) and Gergely Orosz
note: The exact argument that AI raises the value of taste — the 80/20 on setting a quality bar agents can't reach.

title: Now what? Beyond Kubernetes and Cloud Native
note: Knowing when to stop building infrastructure and redirect leverage to product — the "what not to build" discipline.

title: Block CTO Dhanji Prasanna: Building the AI-First Enterprise with Goose
note: How a 4,000-engineer org actually went AI-native: silos to functional teams, open-sourcing the internal agent, swarms of small models over monoliths.

title: Ship AI: Agents, Workflows, and Python — w/ Vercel CTO Malte Ubl
note: Vercel dogfooded production agents (anomaly detection, lead-qual) before shipping the infra — how an infra CTO decides build vs buy vs wait.

title: Engineering practices that make coding agents work
meta: Simon Willison · The Pragmatic Engineer · talk · 28m
note: The exact practices (sandboxing, incremental scope, LLM-as-judge) that make coding agents safe to run unsupervised, from someone shipping 100+ projects via agents.

title: Interrupt 2025 Keynote
note: An honest two-year retrospective on what real agent adoption looks like in production, from the person who builds the framework you ship Skale on.

title: The Agent Development Lifecycle: Build, Test, Deploy, Monitor
note: The build → test → deploy → monitor loop for production agent teams. The operational layer that pairs with the context-engineering pieces for running agents you can actually trust.

title: Building Faster with AI
meta: Andrew Ng · YC AI Startup School · talk · 43m
note: The craft of speed: the edge is the application layer, not models. Prototype ten throwaway ideas in the time others spec one, with tight user feedback loops. He live-builds one in minutes.

title: How to Build a Self-Improving Company with AI
meta: Tom Blomfield · YC Root Access · talk · 13m
note: The frame shift from 'AI as tool' to 'AI as organizational substrate': build loops that regenerate your own operating system. 'Software is ephemeral, context is valuable.'

title: The State of AI: Growth, Fragmentation, and the Next Wave
meta: Martin Casado & Alexandr Wang · a16z · talk · 23m
note: Where value is actually accruing vs hype, the SaaS innovator's dilemma, and why prosumer/brand moats (Cursor-style) are underrated. A tight 23-minute synthesis.

title: Palantir CTO on the SaaS Apocalypse
note: The operator-first, build-for-real-stakes lens, from defense: 'AI without institutional will is useless.' A corrective to pure product-led thinking.

title: Agentic Engineering in Action with Mitchell Hashimoto
note: HashiCorp's founder screen-shares harness engineering on the real Ghostty codebase: build tools, validators and lint rules the agent self-invokes so a class of mistake never recurs, supply the shape of the solution rather than the keystrokes, and run the same task across models on cloned repos to pick the winner empirically.

title: Directing a Swarm of Agents for Fun and Profit
note: A contrarian org-design call from Netflix's former cloud architect: stop hiring application developers, build the platform that operates development, and move headcount to the orchestration-and-guardrails layer. The director does not read the code, he runs the team and nags it to 100% green.

title: Ilya Sutskever — From the age of scaling to the age of research
note: The most direct primary source on what research taste looks like at the frontier: beauty, simplicity, correct inspiration from biological intelligence, and why the paradigm now beats the compute.

title: Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken — How LLMs actually think
note: How two researchers reached the frontier in a year: pick problems adjacent to what works but is poorly understood, then build intuition from where models surprise you.

title: Scaling Test-Time Compute to Multi-Agent Civilizations
note: Noam Brown on recognizing when an existing method (here, the generator-verifier gap) can be generalized into a brand-new scaling axis. This is the move that made o1.

title: John Schulman — Reasoning, RLHF & the plan for AGI
note: Why ChatGPT "could have been built in 2018" — the bottleneck was research imagination, not compute. Read it for what separates groups that find the formulation from those that don't.

title: Ilya Sutskever — NeurIPS 2024 full talk
note: A decade of breakthroughs shown as the same move repeated: notice a fundamental limitation, bet a simple change plus data plus compute resolves it.

title: Andrej Karpathy — AGI is still a decade away
note: The field's most-cited working teacher on real-versus-hype: why it's "the decade of agents, not the year," why RL is a weak signal channel, and how to reason about tractable-but-hard.

title: Yann LeCun — Objective-Driven AI (world models)
note: Meta FAIR's head making the case against scaling autoregressive LLMs (JEPA, energy-based prediction, planning). The contrarian paradigm you have to be able to argue for.

title: Richard Sutton — Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
note: The Bitter Lesson's author arguing LLMs can't learn from experience and continual learning is the real path. Read it against his own essay above to feel a live frontier disagreement.

title: Demis Hassabis — Scaling, AlphaZero atop LLMs, AlphaFold
note: DeepMind's lens: "scaling is an art form," and LLMs as a necessary-but-insufficient world model you bolt search and planning onto. How Hassabis picks the combination instead of betting on scale alone.

title: François Chollet: How We Get To AGI
note: The pretraining era is over; the next bet is test-time adaptation. ARC-AGI as the calibration instrument, from the person who built it.

title: Looking Inside Neural Networks with Mechanistic Interpretability
note: Olah working through how he picked the tractable sub-problem (superposition, circuits) live — research-taste decision-making in motion, not an essay.

title: Gemini Co-Lead on World Models, RL's Next Domains & Continual Learning
note: Gemini's co-lead (and AlphaStar's builder) on where RL goes next, why world models bridge language to planning, and continual learning as the unsolved core.

title: Automating Science: World Models, Scientific Taste, Agent Loops
note: 'Scientific taste' studied head-on — what separates hypothesis-generators that matter — from someone who red-teamed GPT-4 for chemistry and now automates drug discovery.

title: State of LLMs 2026: RLVR, GRPO, Inference Scaling
note: Raschka walking the LLM training-eras timeline (pretraining → RLHF → LoRA → mid-training → RLVR → inference scaling → continual learning) in one focused hour — which axis gets rewarded next.

title: State of AI in 2026 (Lex Fridman #490)
meta: Sebastian Raschka & Nathan Lambert · Lex Fridman · podcast · 4h25m
note: Raschka plus Ai2's post-training lead (RLHF Book author) on where the frontier actually sits: post-training paradigms, scaling-law status, open vs closed, compute economics. The current 'what to bet on' synthesis.

title: Dario Amodei, Chris Olah & Amanda Askell (Lex Fridman #452)
note: Three Anthropic principals in one sitting: Amodei on scaling/timelines, Olah live-explaining interpretability (circuits, superposition, SAEs), Askell on Constitutional AI and model character.

title: Scaling and the Road to Human-Level AI
note: The scaling-laws inventor on why intelligence scales predictably, where the curve still runs, and why the next breakthroughs need paradigm shifts, not just more GPU. The primary source on scaling intuition.

title: Don't Teach. Incentivize.
note: The o1 co-lead's inversion of the teaching frame: design the incentive (verifiable reward), let scale surface the capability. The mental model behind o1 and R1, told by an insider.

title: Sparks of AGI: Early Experiments with GPT-4
note: The methodology of probing a frontier model's real capability surface — breadth-first, qualitative, hunting for limits — instead of chasing benchmarks. How to evaluate emergence honestly.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in Large-Scale Deep Learning
note: The Tensor Programs / muP architect on the math of predicting optimal hyperparameters across scale — the theory behind muTransfer (hyperparameter search at ~7% compute). The mechanistic answer to 'what does correct scaling mean.'

title: Jeff Dean & Noam Shazeer — 25 years at Google: from PageRank to AGI
note: The inventors of the Transformer, MoE, and the modern compute stack on which architectural bets paid off and how to weigh scale vs algorithm. Primary source from the people who built it.

title: Is human data enough?
note: AlphaGo/AlphaZero's lead on why 'the era of human data' is ending and 'the era of experience' (RL from self-play) is the path past human level. From the person who ran the experiments that proved it.

title: The arrival of AGI
note: The person who defined AGI in 2007 revisiting whether the definition holds — Levels of AGI, recognition criteria, and safety as capability climbs. A distinct lens from Hassabis and Silver.

title: AlphaFold: Grand challenge to Nobel Prize
note: How the AlphaFold lead picked a 50-year grand-challenge problem, what made it tractable once nets arrived, and how he structured the bet. A worked example of research method outside NLP.

title: Open Source AI is AI we can Trust
meta: Soumith Chintala (PyTorch / Meta) · Latent Space · podcast · 1h38m
note: The PyTorch creator on why its design ethos (progressive disclosure of complexity, user over research team) beat TensorFlow — the Bitter Lesson applied to frameworks — plus an unguarded map of the open-source stack.

title: Jonathan Frankle: From Lottery Tickets to LLMs
note: From the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis to training 70B models: how he picks problems, the composition problem (which efficiency tricks stack vs cancel), and why doing more per FLOP is the training-side compound-systems principle.

title: Spatial Intelligence is the Next Frontier in AI
meta: Fei-Fei Li · YC AI Startup School · talk · 44m
note: The ImageNet creator modeling how to pick a 10-year research bet: 'avoid problems industry will solve with greater resources.' Spatial intelligence as the next, harder frontier.

title: AI Agents and the Path to AGI
note: The person who led GPT-4 and o1 on how test-time compute became the new scaling axis once pretraining plateaued, and why that specifically unlocks reliable agents.

title: Context Engineering: Lessons from Scaling CoCounsel
meta: Jake Heller (Casetext) · YC Root Access · talk · 20m
note: The hardest-won operator account of turning GPT-4 into a reliable professional product: the demo-to-product gap is entirely context architecture. Define the experience before the prompts.

title: Context Engineering for Engineers
meta: Jeff Huber (Chroma) · YC Root Access · talk · 11m
note: From the person who built the retrieval layer: reliability comes from what you filter OUT as much as what you put in. Gather-and-glean plus compaction, concretely.

title: Why One of OpenAI's Top Researchers Walked Away
note: The RL lead behind o1/o3/Codex on where scaling RL hits real walls, and the structural reason big labs turn conservative exactly when the next paradigm needs a bet. A rare insider account of choosing what to work on and when to leave the consensus path.

title: How OpenAI Shapes Its Research And What's Next
meta: Mark Chen (OpenAI Chief Research Officer) · Core Memory · podcast · 1h38m
note: The person allocating OpenAI's ~300 active projects: where the GPUs go is the research strategy, chasing incremental wins to beat a competitor is a losing way to do research, and the durable edge is cracking the next paradigm rather than catching up on this one. Problem-selection at org scale, from the allocator.

title: Ethan Perez: Bottom-Up Alignment Research
meta: Ethan Perez (Anthropic) · The Inside View · talk · 37m
note: Concrete project-selection heuristics: a month of fixed setup before the first result is a red flag, run quick experiments before reading weeks of prior work, keep alternative directions visible so it stays easy to drop merely-incremental work, and pick collaborators by how much you will learn from them.

title: Fully autonomous robots are much closer than you think
meta: Sergey Levine (Physical Intelligence / Berkeley) · Dwarkesh Patel · podcast · 1h28m
note: Levine's contrarian taste call: RL is not the starting point, you need a large supervised prior before learning from your own experience pays off, which inverts the naive 'just do RL' instinct. He reframes robotics as an Apollo-style industrial build with a compounding data flywheel, not a paper problem.

title: Open-Endedness and General Intelligence
note: The case for open-endedness as the missing ingredient for general intelligence: agents that set their own goals, generate unlimited novel-but-learnable training environments, and close self-improvement loops. A distinct bet on which problem to pick that the section's scaling and world-model entries don't touch.

title: Jack Lindsey on AI 'psychology'
note: How an interpretability lead builds intuition by watching where models break: models plan ahead, emotion features are causal (ablating a 'desperation' neuron stops reward-hacking in code), and training on one narrow bad behavior can summon a general 'evil persona.' Taste built from the run, not the abstract.

title: Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)
note: Karpathy codes GPT-2 124M from an empty file to a model that beats the original on HellaSwag, walking the weight init, residual scaling, mixed precision, gradient accumulation and the exact GPT-2/GPT-3 hyperparameters that separate a real training run from a toy. It assumes you know backprop and teaches the run-level judgment you never get from docs: throughput tricks, debugging by watching the loss, matching a paper's recipe.

title: Let's build the GPT Tokenizer
note: Byte-pair encoding from scratch, and exactly how tokenization causes the bugs that bite in production: broken arithmetic, code and whitespace handling, non-English degradation, trailing-space artifacts, the SolidGoldMagikarp class of failures. The experienced-only view of the layer most people treat as a black box.

title: An Observation on Generalization
note: Ilya teaching how he reasons about why learning works at all: prediction is compression, a network is a computer SGD searches for the shortest program, and unsupervised learning pays off because jointly compressing the data and the task extracts shared structure. The intuition a frontier researcher uses to decide what should work before running it.

title: Stanford CS336: Language Modeling from Scratch
meta: Percy Liang & Tatsunori Hashimoto · course · 17 lectures
note: The closest public thing to a frontier lab's internal curriculum, and the systems craft most engineers skip: resource accounting, GPU kernels and Triton, multi-machine parallelism, scaling laws, MoE, and inference optimization. Strong PyTorch is assumed, so it starts where the explainers stop.

title: Michael Truell: Building Cursor at 23
note: The exact reason they forked VS Code (architectural control the extension API couldn't give) — your blueprint for "own your daily-driver tool as primary R&D."

title: The Future of Software Creation with Replit CEO Amjad Masad
note: The "be the substrate, not the wrapper" thesis stated bluntly — and why reliability at 95% beats capability at 70% when users get burned twice and leave.

title: Figma's CEO: Why AI Makes Design, Craft, and Quality the New Moat
note: When AI commoditizes features, taste is the last moat — extract "removing blockers beats adding features" as a product-prioritization rule.

title: Lessons from building Vercel v0 and the d0 agent
note: The primary source for "don't train your own foundation models; use a composite architecture," from the person who built v0.

title: Linear's sync engine: a synchronous experience with async data
note: Linear's CTO explaining the primitive they built before the product, and exactly how the sync engine produces that instant feel.

title: How Cursor Builds at the Speed of AI
note: The conviction framework behind owning the editor when everyone said build an agent — the tightest, most architectural Truell talk.

title: Retrieval After RAG — Turbopuffer
note: Primitive-first with receipts: three platform shifts (S3 consistency, NVMe, compare-and-swap) had to converge before the architecture was even possible. Powers Cursor and Notion.

title: Building the Generative Web with AI
note: The CEO-level case for just-in-time, generated-on-demand software, and why reliability (users leave after two failures) forced v0's composite architecture.

title: Inside Devin: The AI engineer
note: Scott Wu (competitive-programming world champ at 17) on the 8 pivots before Devin, the conviction that models were production-ready before the market believed it, and treating software engineering as a whole task, not code completion.

title: Mikey Shulman (Suno): The Future of Music
note: The technical decision loop behind an AI-native creative product: why autoregression over diffusion (full-song coherence), why music isn't a scale problem like LLMs, and the 'blank canvas' insight that 90% of users create, not consume.

title: How To Build The Future: Parker Conrad
note: The compound-startup thesis that challenges YC's own 'do one thing' dogma: 'islands of undiscovered PMF no one sails to.' Validated by Rippling's $13.5B.

title: How To Build The Future: Aravind Srinivas
note: Perplexity's zero-to-PMF: killing the ChatGPT-clone impulse and redefining search as 'answer with citations.' Building AI-native against an incumbent.

title: Advanced Context Engineering for Agents
meta: Dexter Horthy (HumanLayer) · YC Root Access · talk · 15m
note: The exact production coding-agent workflow: spec-first, subagents as context-control units, frequent intentional compaction. Aimed straight at your LangGraph stack.

title: Lessons from Building Open Source Libraries
meta: Thomas Wolf (Hugging Face) · YC Root Access · talk · 14m
note: From the person behind Transformers/Datasets/Diffusers: open models are market infrastructure, not competition — the founder opportunity is always the application layer above them.

title: Why AI Moats Still Matter (And How They've Changed)
note: The '19 of 20 AI startups building the same thing will die' framework: differentiation is not defensibility. Moats live in workflow ownership and switching costs, not model access.

title: Business strategy with Hamilton Helmer (author of 7 Powers)
note: All seven powers (scale, network, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource, process), which to pursue at which stage, and moat vs power.

title: OpenAI Codex Team: From Coding Autocomplete to Autonomous Agents
meta: Hanson Wang & Alexander Embiricos (OpenAI Codex) · Sequoia · podcast · 38m
note: The researcher who trained the model on why they trained beyond competitive programming to match real software work, and why building realistic training environments, not better prompts, was the unlock for 30-minute autonomous runs. The verifiable-reward lesson applied to a shipped product.

title: Building Claude Code with Boris Cherny
meta: Boris Cherny (Anthropic) · The Pragmatic Engineer · podcast · 1h38m
note: The creator's deepest build account: the 'product overhang' (capability existed, scaffolding didn't), deleting code on every model release and keeping ~90% self-written so the scaffolding doesn't hobble the model, and choosing Bash as one universal interface over dozens of bespoke tools.

title: No Priors: State Space Models with Cartesia's Albert Gu & Karan Goel
meta: Albert Gu & Karan Goel (Cartesia) · No Priors · podcast · 34m
note: The inventor of S4/Mamba on the bet against the transformer monoculture: state-space models give constant-time-per-token streaming where attention's quadratic cost is fatal, and the future is a ~10:1 SSM-to-attention hybrid with statefulness as the substrate. Sharpens when to bet on a new substrate versus ride the dominant model.

title: FLUX: Flow Matching for Content Creation at Scale
meta: Robin Rombach (Black Forest Labs) · TUM AI Lecture · talk · 1h06m
note: The creator of latent diffusion lays out FLUX: rectified-flow over standard diffusion, an MM-DiT transformer that processes text and image as parallel streams, and adversarial/preference distillation for fast sampling. The canonical builder account of the current image-generation paradigm.

title: Dream Machine: Emergent Capabilities from Video Models
meta: Jiaming Song (Luma AI) · TUM AI Lecture · talk · 53m
note: Luma's chief scientist argues that scaling one video-diffusion model on enough data makes world-model and 3D-consistency behaviors emerge rather than getting hand-engineered, and shows where they come from and what breaks. The Bitter Lesson applied to generative video.

title: Beating Google at Search with Neural PageRank
note: Exa trains a transformer on a link-prediction objective so documents become embeddings instead of keywords, then builds a custom vector DB because off-the-shelf ones cannot filter at web scale. Search rebuilt for agents, not humans, and the link-prediction-as-pretraining move is the whole architecture.

title: How Glean CEO Arvind Jain Solved the Enterprise Search Problem
note: The person who built Google Search on why enterprise search is a different problem: the corpus is mostly private and per-person, so every query must be personalized and permission-aware in real time atop a knowledge graph of people, roles and documents. Why naive enterprise RAG fails.

title: Sierra: Making Customer-Facing AI Agents Delightful
note: Sierra's reliability primitive: models detect their own errors better than they avoid making them, so they chain supervisor agents to compound past the per-model ceiling, and run a conversation simulator that turns every fix into a permanent regression test. Concrete proof you engineer the harness around today's model rather than wait for a better one.

title: How AI Breakout Harvey Is Transforming Legal Services
note: Harvey deliberately attacks the hardest legal work (international M&A) because that is where the defensible position is: the required process expertise is not online and cannot be scraped. Build many narrow workflows, then collapse them into one the agent selects. In vertical AI the moat is captured process knowledge, not the model.

title: Living Lindy: a No-BS Conversation on AI Agents
note: Two years of running agents in the wild: the problem is task ambiguity, not task length (if you could brief an intern with a clear doc, an agent can do it), few-shot gold examples from human corrections beat instructions and fine-tuning, and your tools must not themselves be agentic. The model is for judgment; the scaffolding is deterministic.

title: OpenEvidence: The AI Product Going Viral With Doctors
note: Nadler refuses to fine-tune a frontier generalist for medicine: train smaller models only on ~40M peer-reviewed papers, orchestrate a retrieval/ranking/specialty-router ensemble so every answer is source-cited, refresh the corpus daily, and give it free to clinicians to win distribution. The data-curation-over-monolith bet on a high-stakes vertical.

title: Hippocratic AI: Building the First Safety-First LLM for Healthcare
meta: Munjal Shah (Hippocratic AI) · The MAD Podcast · podcast · 48m
note: The constellation architecture: a primary clinical model supervised by many specialist models plus human-escalation guardrails, scoped deliberately to non-diagnostic conversational care to keep the verifiable-safety envelope tight. Engineering the supervisory system around the model where safety is the ceiling. (2023; the architecture has since grown, but it is the clearest statement of the bet.)

title: The Bitter Lesson Is Coming for Proteins
meta: Alexander Rives (ESM / EvolutionaryScale) · Latent Space · podcast · 1h10m
note: The creator of ESM on the Bitter Lesson hitting biology: a vanilla BERT-like transformer scaled over sequence, structure and function as one token stream beats hand-engineered MSA-dependent specialists, and generates a novel green-fluorescent protein ~500M years off the evolutionary tree. Problem selection and conviction, told by the builder, distinct from AlphaFold.

title: How End-to-End Learning Created Autonomous Driving 2.0
note: Kendall ripped out the hand-engineered self-driving stack, no LiDAR and no HD maps, for a single generalization-first foundation model that ports to new vehicles and cities in weeks. The Bitter Lesson winning in the hardest physical domain, and why the modular stack was a trap, from the person who made the bet in 2017.

title: Any Robot, Any Task, One Brain
note: One foundation model controls quadrupeds, humanoids and arms it never trained on, adapting in-context to body and environment changes, and the counterintuitive trick is making simulation cartoonish and randomized so policies learn to adapt rather than overfit to sim. A real frontier secret about generalization and sim2real.

title: Building Captions
note: Misra's frame for choosing what to build: bounded problems (talking-head video) versus unbounded ones (general intelligence), and why a bounded problem with a proprietary data flywheel is how a small team owns a category instead of wrapping a model. Contrarian against the build-AGI default.

title: Production AI Engineering Starts with Evals
note: Goyal treats evals as an organizational-alignment tool that turns subjective model debates into measurable facts, and engineered on-prem/data-residency from day one when VCs called it stupid, which won Stripe, Airtable and Zapier. A founder-told account of building the eval layer other AI products run on. (Oct 2024.)

title: How to Build a Beloved AI Product: Granola
meta: Chris Pedregal (Granola) · The MAD Podcast · podcast · 1h09m
note: The decisive, irrational-looking calls a two-person team made to win a crowded notetaker niche: cut half the features to expose the core interaction, and refuse to ship a meeting bot or store audio even when investors balked. Privacy-as-trust as the wedge to get users to outsource their memory.

title: A Technical History of Generative Media (Fal.ai)
meta: Gorkem Yurtseven & Batuhan Taskaya (Fal.ai) · Latent Space · podcast · 1h15m
note: Fal's CEO and head of engineering on why diffusion inference is a different compute problem than LLM serving (naive PyTorch gets ~30% of the GPU; they wrote 100+ custom CUDA kernels), and the counterpositioning call behind it: refuse LLM serving, where Google can give the layer away free, and plant the primitive in a net-new market with no incumbent. The moat is being first to optimize each new architecture, not a permanent edge.
